scope: Comparison of all 14 authored explanations and worked transfers against independently frozen answers, exact preset calculations and primary mathematical definitions.

checks.transfer_check: Mode alone is not automatically Markov when age adds predictive information; suitable state augmentation is appropriately conditional on evidence.
B-to-A is 40%, while A-to-B remains 20%; row/column and reverse-conditioning distinctions remain consistent.
[100%,0%,0%] is a valid complete row without smoothing. Mathematical validity is separated from model usefulness.
P(A,C)P(C,A)=0.20×0.40=0.08; this one path is correctly distinguished from the full 0.52 endpoint probability.
25×0.52=13 is an expectation. A possible count of 11 alone does not contradict the model; no exact finite-count or path-frequency guarantee is asserted.
A point mass on B is unchanged before any transitions; its next distribution is row B.
The stated [1/2,1/4,1/4] vector times the mixing matrix is exactly unchanged in every coordinate.
The alternating matrix preserves [1/2,1/4,1/4] while every diagonal is zero; stationary initialization and point-mass initialization are distinguished.
Odd step 9 is [0,1/2,1/2], even step 10 is [1,0,0]. Time averages are explicitly a different operation from a late-step distribution.
All-positive entries imply irreducibility and positive diagonal entries imply period one. The stated stationary distribution is nonuniform; finite rounded plots are not treated as proof.

An absorbing B row is a correct counterexample to universal reachability of A. The concrete absorbing preset additionally supplies routes from B/C to A; gradual growth is not claimed to finish by a fixed finite horizon.
[0.20,0.30,0.50] becomes [0.40,0.60,0] in one step and stays there. Every distribution supported on absorbing A/B is stationary, and initial-state dependence is retained.

conceptual_checks: Finite time-homogeneous Markov conditioning is distinguished from independence and state-description adequacy.
Conditional transition probabilities, particular paths, endpoint distributions, expectations and observed counts remain distinct.
Stationarity concerns distributional invariance and permits individual motion; it is not inferred from rounded plot flatness.
Finite irreducibility is correctly stated as sufficient for stationary uniqueness, without an incorrect necessity claim; aperiodicity is used for all-start convergence.
Periodic counterexample retains its unique stationary distribution while its chosen initial distribution does not converge.
Absorption and multiple closed classes do not imply common limits without the appropriate additional rows and initial-state conditions.
verdict: Accepted: all 14 answer keys match the frozen blind review; every explanation and numerical transfer is correct, and no conceptual overclaim was found.
limits: Content-only review. Explorer validation, lack of random sampling, floating-point computation, UI rendering, integration and native browser behavior are not independently established by this receipt.
